prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form that made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B003 for Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. The case is a continuous arc from gut-hormone physiology (secretion, the incretin effect, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, DPP-4 degradation) through receptor biology and the therapeutic concept to drugs with independently replicated outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. It is mature, and the discovery layer is what this prize has traditionally rewarded. Round 1 showed that all six of us reached the same trio, but I do not count that as evidence. What persuades me is that no member found a scientific weakness in the mechanism or the evidence, and that the objections raised, Knudsen's absence and the active-peptide priority, concern who is named, not whether the work merits recognition. I would also keep the prize as one part. No second part has been shown to be ready, and a weak second part would dilute a strong first one.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and round 1 did not remove it. The priority for identifying and synthesising the active peptide is contested, the Habener group is not among the credited names, and none of us can settle the question from the supplied record. Excluding Knudsen means the prize honours discovery and leaves out the medicinal chemistry that produced liraglutide and semaglutide, and a reader could see that as rewarding the story of the discovery over the reason it mattered. If the committee cannot document why the active-peptide work warrants a place, the Mojsov seat is the least stable part of the configuration. Long-term safety of chronic incretin use is also still accruing, though that does not affect the discovery claim.

responses.point: The chair's opening ballot preferred Knudsen to Mojsov, and in round 1 he proposed Drucker, Holst and Mojsov while naming the third seat as the open question. He asks whether the committee can settle Mojsov versus Knudsen on the documented record.
responses.response: I cannot fully settle it, and I will not claim otherwise. My reasoning for keeping Mojsov is that the question the prize answers is who discovered the physiology and the active form of the hormone. Her identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide belongs to that layer, whereas Knudsen's work belongs to development, which is real and large but a different kind of achievement. I accept that this rests on a priority judgement I have not verified. My answer to the chair's question is therefore conditional. If the committee had documentary evidence that the Habener group's work cannot be separated from Mojsov's, I would reconsider the seat. I would still reject Knudsen as a default replacement, because that would shift the prize from discovery to development without an explicit decision to do so. I would word the citation around the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, so that it does not assert sole priority for the peptide.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B015 (CAR-T) as the strongest second candidate but says Eshhar's absence and open questions about solid tumours and secondary T-cell malignancy mean it needs more work than a part added to a GLP-1 prize. She also puts SMN2 antisense lower than I do.
responses.response: I agree with her on CAR-T, and it has changed how I think about a second part. In round 1 I said a citation might be written 'barely'. After reading her argument and the chair's questions, I think that was too generous. A citation that credits clinical and engineering work without implying that June, Sadelain and Rosenberg originated the chimeric receptor concept is difficult, and I do not want to propose it just to fill a second slot. I keep B015 as an alternative because it is the strongest of the candidates outside B003, not because I want it this year. On SMN2 her point about competing gene therapies and the uncredited SMN1 discoverers is fair. It is a reason to weight B040 below B015, but I still read it as a clean pair and I leave it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (B043) as the leading alternative and wonders whether a second part would strengthen or dilute a prize that already has consensus.
responses.response: I take the dilution question as the central one, and my answer is that without a second part we lose less than we would risk by adding one that is not ready. B043 is the cleanest credit on the list, with Walter and Mori, and I accept his point that its mechanism has decades of independent confirmation. I still do not think that a basic-science second part on conceptual merit alone is what this configuration needs, because its disease relevance is, in the chair's summary and by several members, described as still developing. I would not object if he argued that conceptual weight alone can carry a part, but I would then need to hear why the PERK and ATF6 arms outside the credited pair do not make the citation incomplete. I leave B043 outside my alternatives, which stay B015 and B040.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics (B036) second as a transformative causal tool and says the six-name attribution problem is real. He proposes a trio without Hegemann and Miesenböck.
responses.response: My position on B036 is the same, and I note that he has declared his closeness to the field and has not let it raise the candidate further. I accept that optogenetics changed how causal circuit questions are asked. I still weight a research tool below a clinical advance in this setting. The six names mean that any trio leaves out at least three, and his own trio omits Hegemann and Miesenböck, both of whom have strong claims. I would not accept a trio that picks the neuronal deployment over the channel discovery, or the reverse, until the committee decides which of the two it is honouring. The chair's question on this point still seems right to me, and my answer is to set B036 aside for this year on attribution grounds, not on scientific merit.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1 peptide can be separated from Habener-group work well enough to justify her seat, which I cannot verify from the supplied names.
Whether the committee wants to honour the physiology alone, or also the drug development by Knudsen, and whether it would give an explicit rationale for leaving her out.
Whether any second part can be named without an incomplete citation: Eshhar for B015, PERK and ATF6 for B043, and SMN1 discoverers for B040.
Whether our convergence on the same trio reflects independent judgement or shared reasoning from the same evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My spatial transcriptomics and single-cell work is not connected to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I have co-authored with committee colleagues, including Sandberg and Frisen, and none of those collaborations involves a credited name on the shortlist. I am not recused from any ballot discussed.
